senses.whyHard: Also: a road or path; how to get somewhere. "The way of the ninja" is like "the ninja way of life".

anchors.context: But you have seen the way of the ninja
You have followed the way of the ninja

web.meaning: The thin net a spider makes to catch insects.
web.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
web.example: The spider sat in the middle of its web.
web.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

weed.meaning: A wild plant that grows where you do not want it.
weed.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
weed.example: We pulled the weeds out of the garden.
weed.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

whisper.meaning: To speak very quietly, using your breath, so only people near you can hear.
whisper.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
whisper.example: She whispered the answer to her friend.
whisper.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wildly.meaning: In a fast, excited way, without control.
wildly.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
wildly.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

windowsill.meaning: The flat shelf at the bottom of a window.
windowsill.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
windowsill.example: There is a plant on the windowsill.
windowsill.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wipe.meaning: To clean or dry something by moving a cloth or your hand over it.
wipe.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
wipe.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wise.meaning: Knowing a lot and able to make good choices.
wise.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
wise.example: My grandma is a wise woman.
wise.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

wonder.meaning: To think about something and want to know about it. "I wonder where..." means "I want to know where...".
wonder.usageNote: A common word. Good to learn.
wonder.example: I wonder what time it is.
wonder.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

worthy.meaning: Good enough to get or have something.
worthy.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
worthy.example: He wanted to be worthy of his team.
worthy.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

woven.meaning: Made by crossing long thin pieces (like grass or thread) over and under each other.
woven.usageNote: A common word. Good to know.
woven.example: She has a woven basket for fruit.

wow.meaning: A word you say when you are surprised or think something is great.
wow.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yeah.usageNote: Informal spoken English. Use "yes" in writing.
yeah.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yep.usageNote: Informal spoken English. Do not use it in writing at school.
yep.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yikes.meaning: A word you say when you are surprised or a little afraid.
yikes.usageNote: Informal spoken English, often used by children. Good to understand.
yikes.whyHard: This word is harder than everyday English.

yourselve.meaning: You, the people being spoken to.
yourselve.whyHard: This word is less common than the school words for the same idea.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared
paragraphs.mainIdea: A magic tree house appears in the woods of a small town.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day, a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.

background.note: Frog Creek is a made-up small town. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the United States.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree house was magic.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is magic. It can take Jack and Annie into the places in its books.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie found out that the tree house was magic. When they pointed to a picture in a book and wished to be there, the tree house took them to that place.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie visited the time of dinosaurs, old England, ancient Egypt
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us about Jack and Annie's first four trips.
paragraphs.simple: Before this book, the tree house took Jack and Annie to the time of the dinosaurs, to England long ago, to Egypt thousands of years ago, and to a pirate ship. Each trip is a different book in the series.

background.note: England long ago, in the time of knights and castles.
Egypt more than 3,000 years ago, when its kings and queens built the pyramids.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, they discovered that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She is a magic librarian.
paragraphs.simple: During their trips, Jack and Annie learned that the tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She can do magic, works with books, and comes from the time of King Arthur. She travels to different times and places to collect books.

background.note: A woman who can do magic in the old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is kind and loves books.
A king in old British stories. He and his knights lived in a castle called Camelot. Nobody knows if he was a real person.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie are about to start a whole new adventure
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now a new trip is going to begin, in this book.
paragraphs.simple: Very soon, Jack and Annie will start a new and exciting trip. You can read about it in this book, Night of the Ninjas.
paragraphs.tone: The three dots (…) make you wait a moment, like a little drum roll, before the name of the book.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie were walking home from the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie walk home past the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie were walking home from the library. Their way home went right next to the Frog Creek woods.

background.note: The town where Jack and Annie live. It is not a real town. "Creek" is an American word for a small river.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. “We looked this morning,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is tired of looking.
paragraphs.simple: Jack let out a long breath. He said they had already looked that morning, the day before, and the day before that.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is a little fed up. He says "the day before" again and again to show they have looked many, many times.

paragraphs.context: Jack stared at the woods. He was starting
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is losing hope.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at the woods. He was starting to think that nothing good would happen. Maybe he would never see Morgan again.

paragraphs.context: Weeks had passed. And there had not been
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan and the tree house have been gone for weeks.
paragraphs.simple: Many weeks went by. They saw nothing of Morgan le Fay, and nothing of her magic tree house either.

background.note: A magic woman from old stories about King Arthur of England. In this series she is a kind librarian who owns the magic tree house.

paragraphs.context: Oh, she’s just pretending as usual, Jack thought.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks Annie is pretending, but he is excited.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought Annie was only playing a game again, like she often does. But his heart began to beat fast, because he hoped she was right.

paragraphs.context: “She better not be kidding,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hopes Annie is not joking.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said Annie had better not be joking.
paragraphs.tone: "She better not be kidding" is everyday American speech. It means "I hope she is not joking", and Jack is excited and a little worried.

paragraphs.context: He took off into the woods to find
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack runs into the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack quickly ran into the woods to find Annie.

paragraphs.context: Night was falling fast. Crickets chirped loudly. It
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is getting dark in the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Night was coming fast. Small insects called crickets were making loud sounds. It was hard to see in the dark places under the trees.

paragraphs.context: Annie waved from the window of a tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is back in the tall oak tree.
paragraphs.simple: Annie waved from the window of a tree house. It was in the tallest oak tree in the woods. A long ladder made of rope hung down from it.

paragraphs.context: Jack ran to the rope ladder. He started
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack starts to climb.
paragraphs.simple: Jack ran to the rope ladder and started to climb up.

paragraphs.context: As he climbed, he looked out over the
paragraphs.mainIdea: From the ladder Jack can see the sky is still light.
paragraphs.simple: While he climbed, Jack looked out over the woods. Down in the woods it was dark, but high above the tops of the trees there was still some light.

paragraphs.context: Annie sat in the shadows. Books were scattered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie sits in the dark tree house with books everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was sitting in a dark part of the tree house. Books were lying all over the place.

paragraphs.context: On the floor the letter M glowed in
paragraphs.mainIdea: A glowing letter M is on the floor.
paragraphs.simple: The letter M was shining softly on the floor. The light was not bright. M was short for Morgan le Fay.

paragraphs.context: A little mouse ran out from behind a
paragraphs.mainIdea: A mouse runs out and sits on the M.
paragraphs.simple: A small mouse ran out from behind a pile of books. It ran to the shining M on the floor.

paragraphs.context: Jack had to admit the mouse was cute.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse is cute.
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not really want to say it, but the mouse was cute. It had brown and white hair and big dark eyes.

paragraphs.context: Annie slowly reached out her hand. The mouse
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie touches the mouse.
paragraphs.simple: Annie slowly moved her hand toward the mouse. The mouse stayed still. Annie touched its very small head gently.

paragraphs.context: “You’re nuts, Annie,” said Jack. “Just because the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the mouse is just a normal mouse.
paragraphs.simple: "You are crazy, Annie," said Jack. He said the mouse was not magic just because it was in the tree house. It was a normal mouse that came in by itself.
paragraphs.tone: "You’re nuts" sounds rude, but Jack and Annie are brother and sister. It is a friendly way of saying "That’s silly".

paragraphs.context: Jack went over and picked up the paper.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds a piece of paper with writing on it.
paragraphs.simple: Jack went and picked up the paper. Someone had written on it.

paragraphs.context: “Oh man,” whispered Jack, after he read the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is shocked by what he reads.
paragraphs.simple: Jack read the words. Then he said "Oh man" very quietly, because he was surprised and worried.

paragraphs.context: “A note,” said Jack. “It must be from
paragraphs.mainIdea: The note is from Morgan, and she is in danger.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said it was a note. He thought it was from Morgan, and that she was in a very bad situation.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe she was trying to write things,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks Morgan could not finish a word.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought Morgan was trying to write "things". The last letter n went off the edge of the paper, so the word looked like "thin".

background.note: Morgan’s note is shown as a picture in the book. Her writing goes off the edge of the paper, as if she could not finish.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe the spell was starting to make her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks magic is making Morgan disappear.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said that maybe a magic spell was making Morgan go away, and that is why she could not finish writing.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack. “I wonder if she left
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks for more clues.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agreed. He wanted to know if Morgan left any other things to help them. He looked quickly around the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “Look!” Annie pointed at a book in the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie sees one open book.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed at a book in the corner. It was the only book that was open.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around again. Annie was right. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels a little afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked again. Annie was right. He felt a cold feeling move down his back, because this was strange and a little scary.

paragraphs.context: Jack went over to the book and picked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks at the open book in the evening light.
paragraphs.simple: Jack picked up the book and held it near the window. The sun was going down, and its light made the page look gold.

paragraphs.context: Jack stared at the picture on it. In
paragraphs.mainIdea: The picture shows a mountain with flowering trees and a stream.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at the picture. It showed trees with white flowers on the side of a mountain, near a wide, fast river.

paragraphs.context: Two people were also in the picture. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two people in dark clothes are in the picture.
paragraphs.simple: There were two people in the picture. They wore dark clothes, with black cloth over their faces. Long swords were tied to their backs.

paragraphs.context: “Morgan must have left the book open to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks Morgan opened the book on purpose.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said Morgan surely left the book open at this page because she wanted them to see it.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, Morgan’s in trouble! She needs us now!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to go now to help Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said Morgan was in danger and needed them now.

paragraphs.context: “But we should read this book first,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to read first.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they should read the book first, so they would be ready.
paragraphs.tone: This is the usual difference between them: Jack is careful and likes to read and plan; Annie wants to act at once.

paragraphs.context: “Forget it!” said Annie. “Every minute counts!” She
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says there is no time, and takes the book.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "No!" She said they could not lose a single minute. She took the book away from Jack quickly.

paragraphs.context: “Give it back,” he said. “We have to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack asks for the book back.
paragraphs.simple: Jack told her to give it back. He wanted to learn about the place first.

paragraphs.context: Annie held the book out of reach. “We’ll
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie keeps the book away from Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie held the book where Jack could not get it. She said they would learn about the place when they got there.

paragraphs.context: The leaves of the oak tree began to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The magic is starting.
paragraphs.simple: The leaves of the oak tree began to move.
paragraphs.tone: In every Magic Tree House book, the magic starts like this: wind, shaking leaves, and the tree house spins.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t be scared, Peanut,” said Annie. She scooped
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie takes the mouse with her.
paragraphs.simple: Annie told Peanut not to be afraid. She picked the mouse up in her hands and put it in the big front pocket of her sweatshirt.

paragraphs.context: Annie was already looking out the window. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse looks out of the pocket.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was already looking out of the window. The mouse looked out quickly from her pocket.

paragraphs.context: The tree house was in a tree with
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are on a mountain with flowering trees.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house was in a tree with white flowers. It was in a small group of trees on the side of a mountain. Close by, a wild stream ran fast down the hill.

paragraphs.context: Two ninjas were standing on rocks near the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two ninjas are watching the valley.
paragraphs.simple: Two ninjas stood on rocks near the water. They were looking hard at the low land below.

paragraphs.context: One ninja was tall. The other was short.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The two ninjas look just like the picture.
paragraphs.simple: One ninja was tall and one was short. They wore black clothes, black cloth around their heads, and swords tied to their backs.
paragraphs.tone: The short sentences without a verb ("And swords strapped to their backs.") are like quick pictures. They show what Jack sees, one thing at a time.

paragraphs.context: It was exactly like the picture in the
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is just like the book.
paragraphs.simple: Everything looked the same as the picture in the book.

paragraphs.context: “They might think we’re some kind of enemy,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid the ninjas will think they are enemies.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said very quietly that the ninjas might think they were enemies.

paragraphs.context: He picked up the book. He turned to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack starts to read the ninja book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took the book, turned to the first page, and started to read.

paragraphs.context: Very little is known about the shadowy warriors
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells what we know about ninjas.
paragraphs.simple: We do not know much about ninjas. People who study history think ninjas lived in Japan from about the 1300s to the 1600s. Men and women could be ninjas. Sometimes they fought to keep their families safe. Sometimes strong army leaders paid them to find secrets.

background.note: A country of islands in East Asia, to the east of China and Korea.
That is from about the year 1300 to the year 1700, about 300 to 700 years ago.

paragraphs.context: “Wow,” whispered Jack. “We’re in Japan, hundreds of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows they are in old Japan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Wow" very quietly. They were in Japan, hundreds of years in the past.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his backpack. He pulled out his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets ready to write notes.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his bag and took out his notebook and pencil. He liked to write down short notes. He wrote something.

background.note: Jack’s notes are shown as pictures in the book. In every book he writes down the new facts he learns.

paragraphs.context: Jack peeked over the windowsill. His eyes met
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tall ninja sees Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked quickly over the bottom of the window. The tall ninja looked right back into his eyes.

paragraphs.context: “E-hy!” the ninja cried. He dashed toward the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninja shouts and runs to the tree.
paragraphs.simple: The ninja shouted "E-hy!" and ran fast toward the tree. The other ninja came after him.

background.note: A loud shout of surprise or warning. The writer spells the sound, so it is not a real English word.

paragraphs.context: “We’ve got to do something. Fast!” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to stop the ninjas from climbing up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they had to act fast. He told Annie to pull up the ladder.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie grabbed the top of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: They pull the ladder up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie took hold of the top of the rope ladder and pulled it into the tree house.

paragraphs.context: But the tall ninja leaped at the tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas climb the tree without the ladder.
paragraphs.simple: But the tall ninja jumped at the tree and climbed up it. The short ninja came too. They climbed just like cats!

paragraphs.context: The ninjas climbed into the tree house. Neither
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas come in without a sound.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas climbed into the tree house. Neither of them made any sound.

paragraphs.context: The ninjas pulled iron bands off their hands.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas take off their climbing tools.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas took metal rings off their hands. The rings had sharp points like an animal’s nails.

background.note: Real ninjas may have used tools like this to climb. Sharp metal points on the hands helped them hold on to trees and walls.

paragraphs.context: The ninjas stared at Jack and Annie with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Only the ninjas’ eyes can be seen.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas looked hard at Jack and Annie with dark, sharp eyes. Cloth covered the other parts of their faces.

paragraphs.context: Finally the short ninja nodded once. He put
paragraphs.mainIdea: The short ninja keeps Morgan’s note.
paragraphs.simple: At last the short ninja moved his head down once to say yes. He put the note in his shirt pocket.

paragraphs.context: Neither ninja spoke. Jack wished he could see
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas do not speak.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas said nothing. Jack wanted to see their faces. He could not know what they were thinking.

paragraphs.context: The short ninja tossed the rope ladder back
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas want Jack and Annie to go down.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja threw the rope ladder back out. The tall one pointed down the ladder, and then at Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: Oh boy? Is she nuts? wondered Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks Annie is crazy to be happy.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Oh boy!" because she was excited. Jack could not believe it. He thought she was crazy.
paragraphs.tone: Jack repeats Annie’s words "Oh boy?" because he is surprised: he is afraid, but she is happy.

paragraphs.context: The short ninja darted down the ladder. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninja climbs down very fast, using only his hands.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja went down the ladder very fast, moving one hand past the other. His feet did not touch the steps of the ladder.

paragraphs.context: Jack gasped. The ninjas moved very fast. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas are as fast as spiders.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took a quick, surprised breath. The ninjas moved like spiders coming down fast from their webs.

paragraphs.context: “Now’s our chance to leave,” said Jack. “Quick!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to escape.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said this was their chance to go. He looked for the Pennsylvania book again.

background.note: A book with a picture of Frog Creek, in the state of Pennsylvania in the USA. Jack and Annie need it to wish themselves home.

paragraphs.context: Jack sighed. “Why does this always happen?” he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is unhappy because Annie went with the ninjas.
paragraphs.simple: Jack let out a long breath. He asked himself why this always happens to him.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: Annie always runs into danger first, and Jack always has to follow her.

paragraphs.context: Jack put his notebook and the ninja book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack follows Annie down.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his notebook and the ninja book into his backpack. He pushed his glasses up. Then he went down the ladder.

paragraphs.context: The sun had fallen behind the hills. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sun has gone down.
paragraphs.simple: The sun was now behind the hills. The sky had long lines of red and gold.

paragraphs.context: The mouse peeked out from Annie’s sweatshirt pouch.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse looks out.
paragraphs.simple: The mouse looked out from the front pocket of Annie’s sweatshirt.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t be scared, Peanut,” Annie whispered. “We’ll take
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells the mouse not to be afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Annie quietly told Peanut not to be afraid. They would look after it.

paragraphs.context: Great, thought Jack. But who is going to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is worried about themselves.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought "Great!", but he did not mean it. He asked himself who would look after him and Annie.
paragraphs.tone: "Great" here is said in an unhappy way. Jack means "This is not great at all".

paragraphs.context: The short ninja held Jack’s arm in one
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas lead them in the evening.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja held Jack’s arm and Annie’s arm. He took them through the half-dark evening. The tall ninja walked behind.

paragraphs.context: The ninjas stopped near the rushing water of
paragraphs.mainIdea: They stop at a loud, fast stream.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas stopped near the fast water of the wide stream. The water made a loud noise as it ran down the hill.

paragraphs.context: The short ninja looked at Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninja wants them to cross the stream.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja let go of their arms and pushed them toward the stream.

paragraphs.context: The ninja nodded. Then he and the short
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas start walking across the stream.
paragraphs.simple: The ninja nodded. Then the two ninjas stepped into the wild stream and started walking through the water.

paragraphs.context: “No, we have to follow them!” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to follow, to help Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they must follow the ninjas, to help Morgan.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. She was right.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack agrees.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply to be brave. Annie was right.

paragraphs.context: “I can’t go back in,” said Annie, shivering.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The water is too cold for Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said she could not go back into the water. She was shaking with cold.

paragraphs.context: “Me neither,” said Jack. “I’ll have a heart
paragraphs.mainIdea: The water is too cold for Jack too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he could not go in either. He joked that the cold would make his heart stop.
paragraphs.tone: Jack does not really mean it. "I’ll have a heart attack" is a funny way to say "It is a terrible shock".

paragraphs.context: But the ninja lifted Jack high into the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninja carries Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The ninja picked Jack up high and put him on his shoulder.

paragraphs.context: The short ninja put Annie on his shoulder.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The other ninja carries Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja put Annie on his shoulder.

paragraphs.context: Then the two ninjas stepped into the stream
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas walk through the deep, icy water.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas walked into the stream again. The very cold water went round and round them. It came up to the middle of the short ninja’s body.

paragraphs.context: But the ninjas moved through the stream as
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas move calmly through the water.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas walked through the stream as calmly and smoothly as two big ships with sails.

paragraphs.context: The water grew shallow again. Then they were
paragraphs.mainIdea: They reach the other side.
paragraphs.simple: The water became less deep, and then they were on land. The ninjas put Jack and Annie down.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around, too. A full moon was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moon is coming up over the mountain.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked around. A big round moon was coming up. Dark rocks were here and there on the mountain.

paragraphs.context: Then the ninjas started moving. They went silently
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas walk up the hill quietly.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas started to walk up the hill between the rocks, without any sound.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie followed them. Jack wasn’t afraid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack starts to like the ninjas.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie followed. Jack was not afraid now. He even started to like the ninjas. Maybe they could help them find Morgan.

paragraphs.context: The ninjas moved silently. But Jack and Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie are noisy.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas made no sound, but Jack and Annie made a lot of noise.
paragraphs.tone: A small joke: the ninjas are perfect at being quiet, and the children are not.

paragraphs.context: They panted as they climbed the rocky hillside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Climbing is hard work.
paragraphs.simple: They breathed hard as they climbed the rocky hill. Their wet shoes made soft, wet sounds.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly the ninjas froze. Jack could see their
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas see torches in the valley.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the ninjas stopped and did not move. Their eyes looked quickly here and there. People were talking down in the valley. Jack saw burning sticks of fire in the mist.

paragraphs.context: Jack was too out of breath to speak.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is too tired to talk.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was breathing too hard to speak. And he did not know the answer anyway.

paragraphs.context: They came to a pine forest. Night birds
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk into a pine forest at night.
paragraphs.simple: They came to a forest of pine trees. Birds called in the night. The wind shook the branches.

paragraphs.context: The ninjas moved like ghosts through the forest.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas move like ghosts.
paragraphs.simple: The ninjas moved through the forest quietly, like ghosts. Sometimes you could see them and sometimes you could not.

paragraphs.context: One ninja held out his hand, as if
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas tell them to wait, then go away.
paragraphs.simple: One ninja put out his hand to say "Wait" without words. Then both ninjas went into the dark under the trees and could not be seen.

paragraphs.context: He turned the pages until he came to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds a picture of a cave.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turned the pages until he found a picture of a cave.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes ninjas held meetings in hidden mountain caves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ninjas met in secret caves.
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes ninjas met in caves in the mountains, where no one could find them. There they planned secret jobs.

paragraphs.context: “Oh man,” said Jack, “I bet they went
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is sure the ninjas went into a cave.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he was sure the ninjas went into a hidden cave.

paragraphs.context: Jack turned the page. He stared at a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees a picture of a ninja on a mat.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turned the page. He looked at a picture of a ninja sitting on a mat, and he read.

paragraphs.context: Ninjas took orders from a ninja master. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ninjas obeyed a ninja master.
paragraphs.simple: Ninjas did what their leader, the ninja master, told them. The master was a wise person, and no one knew much about him. He knew many secrets of nature.

paragraphs.context: The short ninja motioned for Jack and Annie
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas take them to a cave.
paragraphs.simple: The short ninja moved his hand to tell Jack and Annie to follow. In the dark there was the opening of a cave.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie went into the cave. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go into the dark cave.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie went into the cave. They followed the ninja through the dark.

paragraphs.context: The back of the cave was lit with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many candles light the back of the cave.
paragraphs.simple: At the back of the cave there were many candles. Shadows moved on the walls like dancers.

paragraphs.context: In the flickering light, Jack saw a dark
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see the ninja master.
paragraphs.simple: In the moving candle light, Jack saw the dark shape of a person. He was sitting on a mat made of grass.

paragraphs.context: The ninja bowed to the master. Then he
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninja shows respect to the master.
paragraphs.simple: The ninja bent forward to the master to show respect. Then he moved to one side.

background.note: In Japan people bow (bend forward) to say hello, thank you, or to show respect.

paragraphs.context: The mouse poked its head out of Annie’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse looks out again.
paragraphs.simple: The mouse pushed its head out of Annie’s pocket.

paragraphs.context: “We’re trying to help our friend Morgan le
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains why they came.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they wanted to help their friend Morgan le Fay. She left them a message.

paragraphs.context: Annie pointed to the short ninja. “We gave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie points at the short ninja.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed to the short ninja and said they gave him the message.

paragraphs.context: The woman ninja’s eyes sparkled. Jack thought she
paragraphs.mainIdea: The short ninja is a woman.
paragraphs.simple: The woman ninja’s eyes were bright and happy. Jack thought she might be smiling under her scarf.
paragraphs.tone: A surprise: Jack and Annie thought the short ninja was a man. The book said "Both men and women were ninjas."

paragraphs.context: “Perhaps I can help you,” he said. “But
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master will help only if they show they are good enough.
paragraphs.simple: The master said he might help them. But first they had to show that they were good enough to get his help.

paragraphs.context: Just then the tall ninja appeared. He made
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tall ninja gives the master a silent message.
paragraphs.simple: Just then the tall ninja came back. He moved his hand to give the master a message without words.

paragraphs.context: “We must go now,” he said. “The samurai
paragraphs.mainIdea: The samurai are near.
paragraphs.simple: The master said they must go now. The samurai were near.

paragraphs.context: “Samurai?” said Jack. He knew that the samurai
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows about samurai.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knew that samurai were strong Japanese fighters who were ready to fight.

background.note: Samurai were fighters in old Japan who worked for a lord. They wore armour and carried two swords. In this story they are fighting the ninja family.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, our family is at war with them,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas are fighting the samurai.
paragraphs.simple: The master said his family was fighting a war with the samurai. They had to leave before the samurai found them.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. You must go alone. And beware of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie must go back alone and be careful.
paragraphs.simple: The master said they must go alone, and be very careful of the samurai.

paragraphs.context: “They will think you are one of us,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The samurai will not be kind.
paragraphs.simple: The master said the samurai would think Jack and Annie were ninjas too. They would not ask any questions, and they would not be kind at all.

paragraphs.context: “But you have seen the way of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now Jack and Annie can use the ninja way.
paragraphs.simple: The master said they had seen how ninjas live and move. Now they could do it themselves.

paragraphs.context: The master turned to Jack. “Your tree house
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is to the east.
paragraphs.simple: The master told Jack that the tree house was in the east. They had to go that way.

paragraphs.context: The two ninjas led Jack and Annie out
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas take them out of the cave.
paragraphs.simple: The two ninjas took Jack and Annie out of the cave, into the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: The tall one pointed at the pine forest.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ninjas go away too.
paragraphs.simple: The tall ninja pointed at the pine forest. Then the ninjas also went into the dark and could not be seen.

paragraphs.context: Annie spoke first. “Well, I guess the tall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie decides which way to go.
paragraphs.simple: Annie spoke first. She thought the tall ninja was pointing east. So she thought that was their way.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Jack. “I need to write some
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to write notes.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Wait." He wanted to write some things down.
paragraphs.tone: Even in danger, Jack stops to write notes. It is a funny part of who he is.

paragraphs.context: He looked at her. She had pulled her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes herself look like a ninja.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at Annie. She had pulled the hood of her sweatshirt over her head and tied the strings tight.

paragraphs.context: “Good idea,” Jack whispered. He pulled his hood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts his hood up too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said quietly that it was a good idea. He pulled his hood up too.

paragraphs.context: Jack put his notebook away. Then he and
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk east.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his notebook away. Then he and Annie went east into the woods.

paragraphs.context: They slipped between trees. And more trees. And
paragraphs.mainIdea: There are trees everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: They moved quietly between the trees. There were more and more trees.

paragraphs.context: All the trees looked the same. Jack got
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not know if they are going the right way.
paragraphs.simple: All the trees looked the same. Jack could not think clearly. Were they still going east?

paragraphs.context: “We can’t just guess,” said Jack. “We have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to be sure.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they could not just guess. They had to know without any doubt.

paragraphs.context: “How do we do that?” said Annie. “We
paragraphs.mainIdea: They have no compass.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked how they could know. They did not have a compass to show the way.

paragraphs.context: He remembered something in a camping book. Now
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack remembers a camping book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembered something from a book about camping. He tried to think what it was.

paragraphs.context: Annie picked up a stick. “Here—” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a stick.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picked up a stick and gave it to Jack.

paragraphs.context: They moved into a moonlit space between the
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find a place with moonlight.
paragraphs.simple: They went to an open place between the dark shadows, where the moon was shining.

paragraphs.context: “The stick’s shadow looks like it’s more than
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack measures the stick’s shadow.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said the shadow of the stick looked longer than six inches (about 15 centimetres). He asked Annie what she thought.

background.note: About 15 centimetres. Americans often measure short lengths in inches.
Jack uses an idea from his camping book: the moon makes a shadow, and the shadow can show you which way to go. Real campers often do this with the sun.

paragraphs.context: “So that way is east!” Jack pointed to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks he has found east.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pointed in a new direction. He said that way was east. Then he said he hoped it was.
paragraphs.tone: "At least I hope it is" is funny: Jack sounds sure, and then he is not sure at all.

paragraphs.context: Soon they were out of the pine woods
paragraphs.mainIdea: They walk down the mountain.
paragraphs.simple: Soon they left the pine woods and walked down the rocky side of the mountain. They went slowly from rock to rock. At last they stopped to rest against a very big rock.

paragraphs.context: There were flames of fire coming up the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The samurai are coming.
paragraphs.simple: There were fires coming up the mountain. It was the samurai!

paragraphs.context: Jack flipped through page after page until he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds a picture of samurai.
paragraphs.simple: Jack turned the pages quickly until he found what he wanted. It was a picture of fighters in armour made of bamboo, holding swords.

background.note: Samurai armour was made of many small pieces tied together. Some of it was made from strong, light materials like bamboo and leather.

paragraphs.context: The samurai were fierce Japanese fighters. They carried
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about samurai.
paragraphs.simple: Samurai were strong Japanese fighters. They carried two swords to kill their enemies.

paragraphs.context: In the moonlight, his bamboo armor was shining.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The samurai’s armour and swords shine.
paragraphs.simple: In the moonlight, the samurai’s armour and his two swords were shining.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie crouched together. Samurai were on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie are trapped.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie bent down close together. There were samurai on both sides of them. They could not get away!

paragraphs.context: Jack pressed against the rock.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack hides against the rock.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushed his body hard against the rock.

paragraphs.context: Oh brother, thought Jack. This was nuts. But
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks it is silly, but he tries.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought, "Oh brother, this is crazy." But he closed his eyes tightly and tried to be part of the rock.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to be as still as the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tries to be like the rock.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tried to be as still, as hard and as quiet as the rock.
paragraphs.tone: The short, repeated sentences ("As solid as the rock. As quiet as the rock.") sound calm and slow, like Jack’s breathing.

paragraphs.context: Soon he started feeling as strong as the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels strong and safe.
paragraphs.simple: Soon Jack felt as strong and as safe as the rock. He wanted to be the rock for all time.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. He felt great—he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels like a real ninja.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply. He felt great. He thought he was becoming more like a ninja every minute, maybe even like a ninja master.

paragraphs.context: And they went east. Down the mountain, between
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go back to the stream.
paragraphs.simple: They walked east, down the mountain between the rocks, until they came to the wide, very cold stream.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked across the stream to the dark
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot see the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked across the stream at the dark trees. The moon shone on their light-coloured flowers. But where was the tree house?

paragraphs.context: The water was crashing and rushing over the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The water is very rough.
paragraphs.simple: The water was hitting the rocks hard and running fast over them.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t be afraid,” said Annie. She patted the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells the mouse to be brave.
paragraphs.simple: Annie told the mouse not to be afraid. She gently touched its head. She told it to be like a ninja too.

paragraphs.context: He took a deep breath and stepped into
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tries to cross and falls.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply and stepped into the stream. The cold water came up to his knees. The strong water pushed him down.

paragraphs.context: Jack grabbed some weeds. He held on tight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack holds on to some plants.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took hold of some wild plants. He held on hard while the water went round him.

paragraphs.context: “Jack!” Annie grabbed Jack’s arms. She helped him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie pulls Jack out.
paragraphs.simple: Annie took hold of Jack’s arms. She helped him get back onto the land at the side of the stream.

paragraphs.context: “That was close!” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack was nearly in big danger.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said that was nearly a disaster.

paragraphs.context: Jack wiped his glasses. Luckily, they hadn’t fallen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack’s glasses are safe.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cleaned his glasses. Luckily they did not fall off in the water.

paragraphs.context: “N-not really,” said Jack, his teeth chattering. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is very, very cold.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he was not really OK. His teeth were knocking together. He was cold all the way through his body.
paragraphs.tone: "N-not" shows Jack’s teeth are shaking, so he cannot say the word clearly.

paragraphs.context: “We’ll drown if we try.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They cannot swim across.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they would die in the water if they tried.

paragraphs.context: “Or fr-freeze to death,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is freezing.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said that, or they would die from the cold.

paragraphs.context: He pulled off the hood of his sweatshirt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not feel like a ninja now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pulled his hood down. He did not feel like a ninja any more.

paragraphs.context: Peanut climbed out of Annie’s sweatshirt pouch and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peanut jumps down.
paragraphs.simple: Peanut climbed out of Annie’s pocket and jumped onto the ground.

paragraphs.context: The mouse scampered away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse runs away.
paragraphs.simple: The mouse ran away with small, quick steps.

paragraphs.context: A moonlit branch had fallen across a narrow
paragraphs.mainIdea: A branch is lying across the stream.
paragraphs.simple: A branch, lit by the moon, had fallen across a thin part of the stream. It touched the land on both sides.

paragraphs.context: The mouse vanished into the tall grass on
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse gets to the other side.
paragraphs.simple: The mouse went into the tall grass on the other side of the stream, and they could not see it any more.

paragraphs.context: “We have to try to cross it,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to cross on the branch.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they had to try to cross on the branch. The master told them to follow nature.

paragraphs.context: “Forget it,” said Jack. “It’s too little. It’ll
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the branch will break.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "No way." The branch was too small. It would break at once.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe if we pretend we’re mice, we can
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has an idea.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said that maybe they could do it if they acted like mice.

paragraphs.context: “If you could be a rock, you can
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells Jack to think like a mouse.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said if Jack could be a rock, he could be a mouse. He just had to be very small, not heavy, and fast.

paragraphs.context: “I guess it was big enough,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thinking the right way helped them.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said the branch was big enough after all. They just had to think in the right way.

paragraphs.context: He was still wet from his fall into
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is wet but happy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was still wet from falling into the stream. But now it did not trouble him.

paragraphs.context: The tree house was outlined against the moonlit
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They could see the dark shape of the tree house against the sky, which was bright with moonlight. It was high in a tree, with white flowers all around.

paragraphs.context: In the distance came the sound of voices.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The samurai are coming back.
paragraphs.simple: Far away they heard people talking. Then Jack saw fire.

paragraphs.context: “Take good care of your little helper,” he
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master gives Peanut back.
paragraphs.simple: The master told Annie to look after her little helper well. He gave the mouse to her.

paragraphs.context: “And take this—” said the master. He held
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master has a present for Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The master said "Take this" and held out his hand to Jack.

paragraphs.context: “This moonstone will help you find your missing
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moonstone will help them find Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: The master said the moonstone would help them find their friend, who was lost.

background.note: A real kind of stone that shines softly, like moonlight. In this story it is the first of the four things they need to help Morgan.

paragraphs.context: “You must go home now,” said the master.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master has the Pennsylvania book.
paragraphs.simple: The master said they must go home now. He picked up the Pennsylvania book and gave it to Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Here,” said the master. “You did not see
paragraphs.mainIdea: They could not see the book before.
paragraphs.simple: The master said the book was here all the time. They did not see it, because in their hearts they knew they had a job to finish first.
paragraphs.tone: This is the lesson of the story: they had to finish their mission before they could go home.

paragraphs.context: The master smiled. “No, my friends. I must
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master will not come; they must find Morgan alone.
paragraphs.simple: The master smiled. He said he must stay. They would get more help later on, but they had to find the way themselves.

paragraphs.context: Then he swung silently down the rope ladder.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master goes down the ladder.
paragraphs.simple: The master went quickly and quietly down the rope ladder. Then he went into the dark night and could not be seen.

paragraphs.context: Jack gripped the stone in his hand. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack holds the stone tightly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack held the stone tightly in his hand. He closed his eyes hard.

paragraphs.context: Then he opened his fist. He stared at
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moonstone is in Jack’s hand.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his hand. He looked at the moonstone. It was clear and smooth, and it almost seemed to give out a soft light.

paragraphs.context: They heard their neighbor’s dog, Henry, bark. They
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hear home sounds.
paragraphs.simple: They heard the dog next door, Henry, and the sound of crickets.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, they could see their dad
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their dad is calling them.
paragraphs.simple: Far away, they could see their dad come out of the house and stand on the porch.

background.note: Many American houses have a porch: a covered place outside the front door where people sit or stand.

paragraphs.context: Jack sat back on his heels. He looked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks at the moonstone again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sat back on his feet and looked at the moonstone again.

paragraphs.context: “I guess we have one of the four
paragraphs.mainIdea: They have one of the four things.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought they had one of the four things Morgan needs.

paragraphs.context: “Wait,” said Annie. She took off one of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie takes off her sock.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Wait." She took off one shoe, took off her sock, and put the shoe back on.

paragraphs.context: “Bed! You know, for Peanut to sleep in.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes a sock bed for Peanut.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said the sock was a bed for Peanut. She picked up the mouse and put it gently inside the sock.

paragraphs.context: She put Peanut gently down on the glowing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie leaves Peanut and Morgan’s note.
paragraphs.simple: Annie put Peanut gently on the shining M. She took Morgan’s note out of her pocket and put it next to the mouse.

paragraphs.context: For a moment, its dark eyes looked old
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mouse looks wise.
paragraphs.simple: For a short time, the mouse’s dark eyes looked old and wise.
paragraphs.tone: This is a hint. Maybe Peanut is not a plain old mouse after all. The writer does not tell us yet.

paragraphs.context: By the time he stepped onto the ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is dark when Jack gets down.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack reached the ground, it was almost totally dark.

paragraphs.context: “Here,” said Annie. Her hand bumped his. He
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds Jack’s hand.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said "Here." Her hand touched his. He held it.

paragraphs.context: Together they took off through the cool, dark
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go home through the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Together they left quickly through the cool, dark woods.

paragraphs.context: They moved silently and swiftly—two shadow warriors returning
paragraphs.mainIdea: They feel like ninjas going home.
paragraphs.simple: They moved quietly and quickly, like two ninja fighters going home.
paragraphs.tone: "Shadow warriors" is another name for ninjas. The ending shows that Jack and Annie have learned the ninja way.

sentences.context: She traveled through time and space, gathering books.
sentences.simple: She went to different times and places, and she collected books.
sentences.main: She traveled through time and space.

parts.text: She traveled through time and space
parts.job: Main part: who and what.
parts.meaning: She went to other times and other places

parts.job: What she did on her trips.
parts.meaning: and she collected books.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part after the comma tells you what she did while she traveled. "Time and space" means different times in history and different places in the world.

sentences.context: Nor had there been one sign of her magic tree house
sentences.simple: They also did not see her magic tree house at all.
sentences.main: There was no sign of the tree house.

parts.job: "Nor" means "and also not". The words "had there been" come in a new order after it.
parts.meaning: And there had not been

parts.text: one sign of her magic tree house
parts.job: What they did not see.
parts.meaning: anything to show that her magic tree house was there.

sentences.grammar: After "Nor" at the start, English puts "had" before "there". Read it as "And there had not been ...". It is the same idea as the sentence before it.

sentences.context: Just because the mouse is in the tree house doesn’t mean it’s magic
sentences.simple: The mouse is in the tree house, but that does not make it magic.
sentences.main: That does not mean it is magic.

parts.text: Just because the mouse is in the tree house
parts.job: The reason that some people may give.
parts.meaning: The mouse is in the tree house, but

parts.job: Main part: Jack says the reason is not good enough.
parts.meaning: that does not show it is magic.

sentences.grammar: "Just because A doesn’t mean B" is a common way to say "A is true, but B is not true because of it". The first part is like the "who" of the sentence.

sentences.context: Morgan must have left the book open to this page for a reason
sentences.simple: Jack is sure that Morgan left the book open at this page on purpose.

parts.text: Morgan must have left the book open
parts.job: Main part. "Must have" + "left" means Jack is almost sure this happened.
parts.meaning: I am sure Morgan left the book open

parts.job: Where in the book.
parts.meaning: at this page

parts.job: Why.
parts.meaning: because she wanted us to see it.

sentences.grammar: "Must have done" talks about the past when you are almost sure: "He must have gone home" = I am almost sure he went home.

sentences.context: Very little is known about the shadowy warriors called ninjas
sentences.simple: We do not know much about the secret fighters called ninjas.
sentences.main: We know very little about ninjas.

parts.job: Main part. Nobody is named: it means "people know very little".
parts.meaning: People do not know much

parts.job: What they do not know about.
parts.meaning: about the secret fighters

parts.job: The name of these fighters.
parts.meaning: who had the name "ninjas".

sentences.grammar: "Is known" does not tell you who knows. It means "people know". "Very little" means "not much". "Called ninjas" tells you their name.

sentences.context: Historians believe that ninjas lived in Japan between the 14th and 17th centuries
sentences.simple: People who study history think ninjas lived in Japan from about the year 1300 to the year 1700.

parts.job: Main part: who and what they think.
parts.meaning: People who study history think

parts.job: What they think.
parts.meaning: that ninjas lived in Japan

parts.job: When.
parts.meaning: from the 1300s to the 1600s.

sentences.grammar: "Believe that ..." tells you what someone thinks. The 14th century is the years 1301 to 1400, so it is easy to be wrong by one: 14th = 1300s.

sentences.context: Sometimes warlords hired them to be spies
sentences.simple: Sometimes strong army leaders paid ninjas to find out secrets for them.

parts.job: Main part. "Them" means the ninjas.
parts.meaning: Sometimes strong leaders paid ninjas to work for them

parts.job: The job they paid them to do.
parts.meaning: as secret watchers who found out about enemies.

sentences.grammar: "Hire someone to be ..." tells you the job. "To be" here means "for this job".

sentences.context: But the ninjas moved through the stream as calmly as two sailing ships
sentences.simple: The ninjas walked through the wild water calmly, like big ships moving on the sea.
sentences.main: The ninjas moved through the stream.

parts.text: But the ninjas moved through the stream
parts.job: Main part. "But" shows a surprise: the water was wild.
parts.meaning: But the ninjas walked through the stream

parts.text: as calmly as two sailing ships
parts.job: A picture to show how they moved.
parts.meaning: very calmly, like two ships with sails.

sentences.grammar: "As ... as ..." compares two things: "as calmly as two sailing ships" = in the same calm way as ships. The writer wants you to see a picture.

sentences.context: One ninja held out his hand, as if to say, Wait
sentences.simple: One ninja put out his hand. It meant "Wait", but he did not say it.
sentences.main: One ninja held out his hand.

parts.text: One ninja held out his hand
parts.job: Main part.
parts.meaning: One ninja put out his hand

parts.job: What he meant without words.
parts.meaning: and it was like saying "Wait".

sentences.grammar: "As if to say ..." tells you the message of a movement. The ninja does not speak; his hand "speaks" for him.

sentences.context: Sometimes ninjas held meetings in hidden mountain caves to plan secret missions
sentences.simple: Sometimes ninjas met in secret caves in the mountains. There they planned secret jobs.

parts.job: Main part. "Hold a meeting" = have a meeting.
parts.meaning: Sometimes ninjas met

parts.job: Where.
parts.meaning: in caves in the mountains that no one could find

parts.job: Why.
parts.meaning: so they could plan secret jobs.

sentences.grammar: "To + verb" at the end often tells you why: "to plan" = so that they could plan. "Hidden mountain caves" = caves that are hidden in the mountains.

sentences.context: The master was a mysterious wise person who knew many secrets of nature
sentences.simple: Nobody knew much about the master. He was wise and knew many secrets of the natural world.
sentences.main: The master was a wise person.

parts.text: The master was a mysterious wise person
parts.job: Main part.
parts.meaning: The master was a wise person, and people knew little about him

parts.text: who knew many secrets of nature
parts.job: More about the person. "Who" = this person.
parts.meaning: He knew many secrets of the natural world.

sentences.grammar: "Who ..." after a person tells you more about that person. Read it as a new short sentence: "He knew many secrets of nature."

sentences.context: But first you must prove yourselves worthy of my help
sentences.simple: But first you have to show that you are good enough for me to help you.

parts.text: But first you must prove yourselves
parts.job: Main part. "Yourselves" means Jack and Annie.
parts.meaning: But first you two have to show

parts.job: What they must show.
parts.meaning: that you are good enough to get my help.

sentences.grammar: "Prove yourself" means show that you are good enough. "Yourselves" is for more than one person. "Worthy of" = good enough for.

sentences.context: They will ask you no questions. They will show you no mercy
sentences.simple: The samurai will not ask you any questions. They will not be kind to you at all.
sentences.main: They will not ask or be kind.

parts.text: They will ask you no questions.
parts.job: First thing the samurai will do. "No questions" = not any questions.
parts.meaning: They will not ask you anything.

parts.text: They will show you no mercy
parts.job: Second thing. "Show mercy" = be kind to someone you could hurt.
parts.meaning: They will not be kind to you at all.

sentences.grammar: "Ask you no questions" is a strong way of saying "not ask you any questions". The two sentences have the same shape, which makes them sound strong and scary.

sentences.context: Jack flipped through page after page until he found what he was looking for
sentences.simple: Jack turned many pages quickly. He stopped when he found the thing he wanted.
sentences.main: Jack flipped through page after page.

parts.text: Jack flipped through page after page
parts.job: Main part. "Page after page" means many pages, one after another.
parts.meaning: Jack quickly turned many pages

parts.job: When he stopped.
parts.meaning: and stopped when he found

parts.job: The thing he found. "What" = the thing that.
parts.meaning: the thing he wanted.

sentences.grammar: "Until" tells you when something stops. "What he was looking for" = "the thing that he was looking for".

sentences.context: Because your heart knew you had a mission to complete first
sentences.simple: Deep inside, you knew you had an important job to finish first.

parts.job: The reason. "Your heart" means the feelings deep inside you.
parts.meaning: Because deep inside you knew

parts.text: you had a mission to complete first
parts.job: What they knew.
parts.meaning: that you had an important job to finish first.

sentences.grammar: This sentence starts with "Because". It finishes the sentence before it: "You did not see it before, because ...". Writers sometimes do this to make a short, strong sentence.

sentences.context: There will be more help along the way. But you must find the way on your own
sentences.simple: You will get more help later. But you have to find the way yourselves.
sentences.main: You must find the way on your own.

parts.text: There will be more help along the way.
parts.job: A promise about later.
parts.meaning: People will help you again later.

parts.text: But you must find the way on your own
parts.job: Main part. "But" shows the other side.
parts.meaning: But you have to find the way yourselves.

sentences.grammar: "Along the way" means "while you are on your trip". Look at "way" two times: first it means the trip, then it means how to do it. "On your own" = alone.

sentences.context: They moved silently and swiftly—two shadow warriors returning home
sentences.simple: They walked quietly and quickly, like two ninjas going home.

parts.job: Main part: how they moved.
parts.meaning: They walked without a sound, and fast

parts.job: Who they were like. The long line (—) means "like this:".
parts.meaning: like two ninjas going home.

sentences.grammar: The long line (—) adds a picture of them. "Shadow warriors" means ninjas, so the writer says Jack and Annie are now like ninjas.

take off.meaning: (1) (informal) To leave or run away quickly and suddenly. (2) To remove clothes or shoes from your body.
take off.example: She took off into the woods.
take off.usageNote: Very common. It also means a plane leaving the ground, or taking off your clothes.

lose hope.meaning: To stop believing that something good will happen.
lose hope.example: He was starting to lose hope.
lose hope.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as usual.meaning: In the same way as always.
as usual.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

oh man.meaning: A thing you say when you are surprised, excited or worried (informal, American English).
oh man.usageNote: Informal spoken English. Jack says it a lot.

stand for.meaning: (of a letter) To be the short form of a word or name.
stand for.example: The M stood for Morgan le Fay.
stand for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

reach out.meaning: To move your hand toward something to touch or take it.
reach out.example: Annie slowly reached out her hand.
reach out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

oh brother.meaning: A thing you say when you think something is silly or annoying (informal, American English).
oh brother.usageNote: Informal spoken English. It has nothing to do with a real brother.

pick up.meaning: To take something in your hand and lift it.
pick up.example: Jack went over and picked up the paper.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in trouble.meaning: In a bad or dangerous situation.
in trouble.example: I think she’s in big trouble!
in trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sort of.example: See how the n sort of runs off the page?
sort of.usageNote: Very common in speaking. Not for formal writing.

for a reason.meaning: Because of a reason; on purpose.
for a reason.example: Morgan must have left the book open to this page for a reason
for a reason.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: We have to find out about this place.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

forget it.meaning: A thing you say to mean "No, I will not do that" or "That is not important".
forget it.usageNote: Spoken English. It can sound a little rude.

out of reach.meaning: Too far away to touch or take.
out of reach.example: Annie held the book out of reach.
out of reach.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

scoop up.meaning: To pick something up quickly with your hands curved like a cup.
scoop up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

except for.example: Except for the sound of rushing water.
except for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take notes.meaning: To write down short notes so you remember things.
take notes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pull up.meaning: To pull something up to a higher place.
pull up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

uh oh.meaning: A thing you say when you see that something bad may happen.

oh boy.meaning: A thing you say when you are excited or surprised (informal).
oh boy.usageNote: Informal spoken English. Annie is excited; Jack is not.

hand over hand.meaning: Moving one hand past the other again and again, to climb up or down a rope.
hand over hand.usageNote: You only need to understand it here.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let go of.example: He let go of their arms.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for someone’s sake.meaning: To help someone; because of someone.
for someone’s sake.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm or brave.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

heart attack.meaning: A sudden, serious problem with the heart. People also say it as a joke when something is a big shock.
heart attack.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. It is used to add something stronger.
in fact.example: In fact, he was starting to like them.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out of breath.meaning: Breathing hard and fast, for example after running or climbing.
out of breath.example: Jack was too out of breath to speak.
out of breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep up.meaning: To move as fast as someone else so you are not left behind.
keep up.example: Jack and Annie struggled to keep up.
keep up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come to a stop.example: Finally the ninjas came to a stop.
come to a stop.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand or something in your hand toward someone.
hold out.example: One ninja held out his hand
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as if.meaning: In a way that shows something, though it is not said or not true.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

i bet.example: I bet they went inside a hidden cave.

take orders.meaning: To do what someone tells you to do.
take orders.example: Ninjas took orders from a ninja master.
take orders.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

make a sign.meaning: To move your hand or body to give someone a message without words.
make a sign.example: He made a sign to the master.
make a sign.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

at war.example: our family is at war with them
at war.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

show no mercy.meaning: To be not kind at all; to hurt someone without stopping.
show no mercy.example: They will show you no mercy.
show no mercy.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

i guess.meaning: I think; I suppose (informal, American English).
i guess.example: I guess the tall ninja was pointing to the east

for sure.example: We have to know for sure.
for sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at least.meaning: Here: anyway; even if nothing else is true.
at least.example: At least I hope it is.
at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.
flip through.example: Jack flipped through page after page
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

cut down.meaning: To kill or hurt someone in a fight, usually with a sword.
cut down.usageNote: This meaning is old. Today "cut down" usually means to make a tree fall, or to eat or use less of something.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or excited.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

knock over.meaning: To hit someone or something so that they fall.
knock over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

hold on.meaning: To hold something tightly so you do not fall.
hold on.example: He held on tight as water swirled around him.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

freeze to death.meaning: To die because of the cold. People also say it when they are very, very cold.
freeze to death.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

that was close.meaning: Something bad nearly happened, but it did not.

chilled to the bone.example: He was chilled to the bone.
chilled to the bone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

be supposed to.meaning: Should; to have to do something because you were told or because it is the rule.
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the distance.example: In the distance came the sound of voices.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

along the way.meaning: While you are going somewhere or doing something.
along the way.example: There will be more help along the way.
along the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

on your own.example: But you must find the way on your own.
on your own.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sit back on your heels.meaning: To kneel and then sit on the backs of your feet.
sit back on your heels.example: Jack sat back on his heels.
sit back on your heels.usageNote: You only need to understand it here.

night night.meaning: A thing people say to small children at bedtime; goodnight.
night night.usageNote: A word for small children or pets. It sounds sweet.

pull on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag quickly.
pull on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

about to.meaning: Going to do something very soon.
about to.example: I was about to call you.
about to.usageNote: Very common. "I was about to call you" means "I was going to call you right then".
